hints: Think about what ammonia does when it meets water, does water act as an acid or a base toward it?
Remember ammonia is a weak base, so it accepts a proton from water to form a small amount of hydroxide ions.
Since the reaction is reversible and only goes a little way, decide which two nitrogen species must coexist in equilibrium.
walkthrough:
**Recall how ammonia behaves in water**

Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it acts as a base and accepts a proton, $\text{H}^+$, from water.

Water therefore acts as an acid here, not as a reagent to remove a proton from ammonia.

**Write the equilibrium equation**

The reaction is reversible and only partial because ammonia is a weak base.

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

**Identify the nitrogen species present**

Most $\text{NH}_3$ stays as simple covalent molecules, but a small proportion forms $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions.

There is no formation of $\text{NH}_2^-$ ions, because that would need $\text{NH}_3$ to act as an acid, which does not happen with water.

options.A: Incorrect. Amide ions, $\text{NH}_2^-$, form when ammonia loses a proton and acts as an acid. Water is not a strong enough base to do this, water donates a proton to ammonia instead.
options.B: Correct. In aqueous solution the equilibrium $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$ is set up. Because ammonia is a weak base, most remains as $\text{NH}_3$ molecules with a small amount of $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions present.
options.C: Incorrect. While most dissolved ammonia remains as $\text{NH}_3$ molecules, a small reversible reaction with water always produces some $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$, which is why the solution is weakly alkaline.
options.D: Incorrect. Ammonia is only partially ionised in water. It is a weak base, so conversion to $\text{NH}_4^+$ is far from complete and plenty of unreacted $\text{NH}_3$ molecules remain.
